draft.title: The genetic code
card: The genetic code is the set of rules that turns the order of bases in a gene into the order of amino acids in a polypeptide.
The code is read in triplets. Each group of three bases in mRNA is a codon, and a codon codes for one amino acid or for a stop signal.
Most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon. This is called redundancy, and it means different codons can give the same amino acid.
The code is the same in almost all living things. This is called being universal, so a human gene can be read by a bacterium.
draft.remember: Three bases make a codon, and the same code is used by nearly all life.

a.q: A section of mRNA has 18 bases in a row, all read as codons. How many codons does it contain?
a.why: Each codon is three bases, so 18 ÷ 3 = 6 codons. Choosing 18 treats each base as its own codon, but the code is read in triplets.
a.clue: Divide the number of bases by the size of one codon.

b.q: Two mRNA codons differ by one base but both code for the amino acid leucine. Which feature of the code does this show?
opts: More than one codon can code for one amino acid
Each codon codes for more than one amino acid
One base codes for one amino acid
The code differs between species of organism
b.why: Two different codons giving the same amino acid shows that the code has more than one codon for most amino acids. It is not the reverse: each codon still codes for just one amino acid.
b.clue: Two different codons give the same result.

b.best: More than one codon can code for one amino acid

problems.detail: 'So a human gene can be read by a bacterium' is misleading. Human genes contain introns and bacteria cannot splice them, so a bacterium cannot correctly express a human gene as it is. In practice an intron-free copy (cDNA) is inserted. Better wording: 'so a bacterium can translate human mRNA codons into the same amino acids.'

check.summary: Both questions are sound. The card's claim that a bacterium can read a human gene overlooks introns and should be reworded to refer to the code or to intron-free DNA.
